group.passage:
Between June and October 2015, fires swept across Indonesia. About 2.6 million hectares burned, an area four and a half times the size of the island of Bali, and the smoke closed schools and caused more than 500,000 cases of breathing illness. Many of the fires were set on purpose to clear land for farming, but a long drought helped them spread far beyond what anyone intended. About a third of the burned area was peatland, and there it was not only the plants that caught fire but the ground itself.
Peat forms where land stays soaked with water all year. Because the water keeps out most of the oxygen, dead plants decay so slowly that they pile up instead of rotting away, building a soil that is more than 95 percent water. In Europe, peat grows on average by only about a millimeter a year. Peatlands cover just 3 percent of the world's land, yet they hold more carbon than all the other plant life on Earth combined, forests included.
As long as peat stays wet, its carbon stays locked away. The trouble begins when people dig ditches to drain it for farms and plantations. Air then reaches the peat, which breaks down and releases carbon dioxide, and the ground slowly sinks, in tropical regions by 3 to 5 centimeters a year. Dry peat also catches fire easily. Instead of blazing briefly and moving on, a peat fire can smolder underground for weeks or even months, sometimes surviving days of rain or a layer of snow. Often only a rising water level finally puts it out. During an earlier drought in Indonesia, most fires broke out in peatlands that had been drained or logged, while untouched peat swamp forest stayed at low risk of burning.
Damaged peatlands make up only 0.3 percent of the world's land, yet they produce almost 5 percent of the carbon dioxide released by human activity. A burned forest can slowly take back its carbon as new trees grow, but a peat fire destroys in a single season what took thousands of years to build. For peatlands, then, the best protection against fire is not a fire engine but water.

translation_zh.text:
2015 年 6 月到 10 月，大火橫掃印尼。約 260 萬公頃的土地被燒毀，面積是峇里島的四倍半；濃煙迫使學校停課，並造成超過 50 萬例呼吸道疾病。許多火是為了整地耕作而故意放的，但長期乾旱讓火勢擴散到遠超出任何人的預期。燒毀面積中大約三分之一是泥炭地，在那裡著火的不只是植物，還有地面本身。
泥炭形成於終年泡在水裡的土地。由於水隔絕了大部分的氧氣，死去的植物分解得非常慢，於是一層層堆積起來而不會腐爛消失，形成含水量超過 95% 的土壤。在歐洲，泥炭平均每年只增加約一毫米。泥炭地只占全世界陸地的 3%，儲存的碳卻比地球上其他所有植物加起來還多，森林也包括在內。
只要泥炭保持潮濕，它的碳就會被鎖住。麻煩始於人們挖溝排水，把泥炭地改成農田和種植園。空氣接觸到泥炭後，泥炭會分解並釋放二氧化碳，地面也會慢慢下陷，在熱帶地區每年下陷 3 到 5 公分。乾燥的泥炭也很容易著火。泥炭火不是燒一下就往前移動，而是可以在地底悶燒好幾週甚至好幾個月，有時下了幾天雨或蓋上一層雪都還撐得過去。往往只有水位上升才能把它完全熄滅。在印尼較早的一次乾旱中，大多數的火都發生在被排水或伐木過的泥炭地，而未受干擾的泥炭沼澤森林起火的風險一直很低。
受損的泥炭地只占全世界陸地的 0.3%，卻產生了人類活動所排放二氧化碳的將近 5%。燒毀的森林可以隨著新樹長大，慢慢把碳收回來；泥炭火卻在一季之內毀掉花了數千年才累積起來的東西。因此，對泥炭地來說，防火最好的保護不是消防車，而是水。

open_tasks.prompt: A company plans to drain a peatland to grow crops and promises to plant trees somewhere else to make up for the lost carbon. Based on the passage, write 1–2 English sentences explaining whether this is a fair trade.
reference_answers: It is not a fair trade, because drained peat keeps releasing carbon and may burn, while new trees take a long time to store carbon that the peat built up over thousands of years.
Planting trees elsewhere cannot make up for the loss, since a peatland holds more carbon than forests and becomes a fire risk once it dries out.
